newsitem.title: USA: Clinton proposes bailout of nation's capital.
newsitem.headline: Clinton proposes bailout of nation's capital.

text.p: Saying the government of the nation's capital city had not managed itself well, the White House proposed on Tuesday a partial U.S. takeover of city functions in a bid to rescue the crumbling District of Columbia.

U.S. officials unveiled a $3.9 billion, five-year plan of "tough love" under which the federal government would pick up the tab for a host of programmes now run by the city, including its ageing prisons, crowded courts and potholed roads.
In exchange, Washington D.C. would have to give up its annual federal payment of $660 million and balance its budget by fiscal year 1998.

More significantly, the city would relinquish some of the self-rule it gained from Congress two decades ago -- just the opposite of what advocates of statehood for the District had hoped for when U.S. President Bill Clinton, who seemed sympathetic to their cause, was elected in 1992.

"It's now very plain to everyone that the federal government's relationship with the District is fundamentally flawed," Clinton's budget director Franklin Raines told a news conference. "The local, county and state responsibilities that we gave this city in 1974 have proven to be beyond the city's resources to deal with them.
"Local officials have not performed as well as they must in managing the city," Raines said.
"We view this plan as a plan of tough love. We want to help the District, but we'll insist that the District take specific steps to help itself," Rainse said.

The plan must be approved by Congress, where critics immediately pointed out that it was a net financial gain for the District -- a "bailout for a mismanaged city," as North Carolina Republican Sen. Lauch Faircloth said.
"From the few details I have seen, I like a greater federal role in District affairs. However, this plan could be called the 'great rip off,' not the 'great swap'," Faircloth said.
Raines said the plan would save the city about $770 million over five years, while its net cost to the federal government over that time would be $339 million.
Faircloth said this would increase the federal deficit, a charge Raines' spokesman, Lawrence Haas, denied. But Haas did not say how the White House proposed to pay for its plan.
Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin, who announced the plan with Raines, said Clinton still favours D.C. statehood.
But Raines said that while U.S. officials wanted to improve the prospects for home rule to succeed in Washington, the goal of statehood could not be discussed.
"I think that no matter what your view is on future governance, unless the city and until the city can get its house in order, that discussion will not be successfully engaged," Raines said.
Behind its tourist attractions -- the White House, the monuments and the museums -- Washington is a city of 543,000 that has lurched from crisis to crisis in recent years.

It is plagued by a high crime rate -- 19 homicides have already been recorded in the new year. A former Army general has been brought in to manage the schools, many of which have metal-detectors to keep students from carrying guns inside.

Streets have axle-breaking potholes like those of a Third World country. Heavy snow last winter overwhelmed ill-equipped road crews, producing the comical result that many sidewalks were shoveled by residents while streets were left unplowed.

Meanwhile, Washington has no state government to help it pay for things. It has to pay part of the bill for some programmes, such as Medicaid, the federal health care programme for the poor, that most other cities don't have to finance.

The plan was welcomed by the D.C. delegate to Congress, Eleanor Holmes Norton, and Andrew Brimmer, head of a financial control board appointed to revamp the city government. Mayor Marion Barry said he was encouraged by the move and wrote a letter to the White House commending Clinton's "bold action."
